title: Runtime safety layers: retry, circuit, and KV-eviction heuristics
body:
Summary and intent:

This doc collects a set of proposed runtime safety layers for handling resource exhaustion and transient failures in the serving runtime. It focuses on heuristics and lightweight protocols that sit between the scheduler, kernel selection, and KV cache to: detect impending problems early, contain impact to minimal subset of requests, and recover with minimal duplicated work and predictable latency/cost consequences.

We are targeting production constraints: single-digit ms median latency for short responses, SLOs for p50/p90/p99, and strong isolation between high-throughput customers. The strategies below emphasize: graceful degradation, explicit observability hooks, and cheap fallbacks (software-only before we evict or preempt GPUs).

Design principles (short):
- Layered safety net: detection -> containment -> recovery.
- Fast path remains unchanged for healthy requests; slow/fallback paths used opportunistically.
- Prefer bounded retries with idempotency markers over blind retries.
- Avoid global kill-switches; make circuit breakers per-routing-key/model-variant/instance-group.
- KV cache should expose a "grace window" for recoverable requests so we can resume work without full cache warmup.

1) Detection: continuous headroom estimation
- Each worker exposes a tiny probe that estimates memory headroom and transient allocation pressure. Probe metrics: current_heap_mb, kv_cache_mb, kv_entries, active_sequences, avg_seq_len_last_1m, open_requests.
- Maintain an EWMA of allocation_latency and allocation_failure_rate per-10s bucket.
- If allocation_latency rises > 3x baseline OR allocation_failure_rate > 0.5% -> mark worker as under-pressure (yellow).

2) Containment: request scoring and micro-backpressure
- Assign an in-flight risk score to each request: R = f(seq_len_est, model_variant_cost, user_priority, requires_kv). Simple integer 0..10.
- Admission control policy: accept requests while sum(R) + estimated_future_alloc <= headroom_threshold. Reject/queue low-priority if over threshold.
- For already accepted requests when worker transitions to yellow: start applying per-request mitigations in order of increasing intrusiveness: 1) disable prefetch of KV keys not needed for first N tokens, 2) switch to conservative kernel variant (slower but lower peak memory), 3) enable KV soft-eviction for shadow entries (see KV section), 4) if still critical, trigger soft-reject that returns an explicit 503-with-retry-hint.

3) Micro-fallback ladder (ordered):
- Kernel fallback: runtime can switch from the default attention kernel to an alternate kernel path that uses tiled attention with lower peak working set (approx -20-35% RAM) at ~10-30% throughput loss. This is always per-request, not global. Kernel selection should be precompiled and hot-switchable.
- Model variant fallback: if a quantized or 7-bit compatible variant is available and passes quality guardrails, route the request to that model variant with a flagged response header.
- Replica fallback: route to a different replica group/zone with spare headroom if latency budget allows.
- Managed rejection: best-effort response with explicit retry-after header and a small backoff token for client to avoid thundering herd.

4) KV cache behavior and "grace window"
- KV entries have states: hot, warm, shadow. Shadow entries are soft-evictable: they can be discarded under memory pressure but can be recreated faster because we keep compact deltas on local SSD or a compressed LRU log.
- Grace window: when a request is in progress and requires KV hits, we pin the necessary keys in memory for the duration plus a short grace TTL (default 5s). If the worker needs to evict, it will prefer shadowifying entries older than grace TTL first.
- Checkpoint-on-fallback: before switching kernel or evicting critical KV, we attempt to serialize a minimal checkpoint for the request: (partial decoder position, small hash of KV keys, minimal KV deltas). This enables replay on another worker without re-computing full prefix. Checkpoints are stored in ephemeral fast storage (ramdisk or NVMe cache).

5) Retry semantics and idempotency controls
- Surface an idempotency token for every request (client side or generated at the ingress). Retries should be tied to this token.
- For retried requests, runtime uses cached checkpoints/partial outputs to resume rather than restarting from zero when possible.
- Retry policy (default): on transient errors (OOM, allocation timeout, network transient) retry up to 2 times with jittered backoff (200ms, 500ms). For requests with long expected compute (>2s), prefer a single retry with a heavier fallback (kernel/model fallback).

6) Circuit breakers and escalation rules
- Breakers are hierarchical: per-worker -> per-replica-group -> per-model-variant -> per-routing-key. Each breaker uses: slidingWindowFailures (60s), failThreshold (%), minRequests.
- When a breaker trips at a scope, incrementally widen fallback scope: e.g., tripping per-worker breaker triggers kernel fallback on that worker; tripping per-variant trips will route new requests to alternate variant or degrade QoS.
- Breaker state must be observable and exported as traces for each request that sees a fallback. Include reason tags: oom, alloc_latency, kv_hot_steal, kernel_error.

7) Observability and SLOs to measure effectiveness
- Metrics to emit (per-worker & aggregate): fallback_count_by_type, fallback_latency_delta_ms, checkpoint_write_ms, kv_shadow_evictions, headroom_percentiles, idempotent_replay_hit_rate, retry_count_by_cause.
- SLO targets to track: <1% of requests see managed rejection, p99 fallback latency delta < 300ms on short responses, checkpoint write latency < 50ms, idempotent replay avoids full recompute >80% for retries.
- Health dashboard tiles: headroom heatmap, per-variant circuit state, checkpoint store saturation, KV shadow ratio.

8) Safety checklist for rollout
- Unit tests: kernel-switch unit tests with mocked memory pressure and measured peak allocations.
- Integration: simulate steady-state high-throughput with randomized long-tail sequences, flip worker to yellow and verify fallbacks kick in and SLOs maintained.
- Chaos: forced OOMs on non-prod canary to validate checkpoint/replay path. Observe no customer-visible 5xx beyond expected baseline.
- Perf: measure p50/p95/p99 for both default and fallback kernels and ensure fallbacks are within acceptable cost tradeoff.

9) Open questions and risks (short)
- Checkpoint size and serialization cost: if checkpoints are large we can negate benefit. Need experiments for compact delta formats per-arch.
- Client-level semantics: some customers may not want opaque model-variant fallbacks. Need clear opt-out flags and sticky variant pins.
- KV warmup vs. cost: keeping shadow logs increases write pressure on local NVMe; need lifecycle policy.
- Coordinating cross-worker replays for long conversations: how to guarantee consistent KV state across workers during replay? Use monotonic keys + mutation logs?

10) Next actions and experiments (concrete)
- Experiment A: implement per-request kernel fallback toggle and run canary on 10% traffic for one model. Collect fallback delta metrics. (owner: Marco)
- Experiment B: implement checkpoint proto and ramdisk write/read latency harness; aim for <30ms median. (owner: Samantha)
- Experiment C: KV shadow prototype that writes compact LRU log to NVMe and measures warmup time (owner: Diego)
- Follow-up: design API for clients to express fallback tolerances (force_variant, allow_variant_fallback=false).

Appendix: simple pseudo-flow for request handling under pressure
- ingress -> assign idempotency token -> route to chosen worker -> worker checks headroom -> if OK, continue default kernel
- if worker becomes yellow mid-request -> write checkpoint, switch kernel, shadowify some KV entries, continue. If allocation fails after kernel switch -> attempt checkpoint copy to candidate replica and respond with early 503+retry-token if no candidate available.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic and blends safeguards across layers. I'm expecting discussion on the acceptable UX surface for variant fallback and the size/placement of checkpoints. Please comment with alternatives, especially around checkpoint content and fast storage choices.

-- end --
